HCBCOGN312.topics: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

candidateDecisions.label: Frisian proficiency and field-specific Frisian studies
candidateDecisions.assessment: UCR offers one introductory Dutch course but no Frisian course, cumulative Frisian proficiency sequence, Old Frisian, Frisian linguistics, Frisian literary history, field internship or thesis in Frisian. General psycholinguistics, stylistics, literature and regional politics cannot be presented as Frisian studies.

stoppingDecision.assessment: Three options develop distinct parts of the evidence: language and public communication, cultural interpretation, and heritage and political institutions. These related fields do not supply Frisian proficiency or the specialised regional curriculum. A fourth, Frisian-specific option fails on academic content.

analysis: The closest option directly responds to language study through introductory Dutch, stylistics and cognitive poetics, and psycholinguistics with bilingualism, language acquisition and speech. Rhetoric and applied communication support the public use of language. Sociology and qualitative methods provide genuine contexts and methods for investigating language in society. The literature and media option has its own progression in interpretation, literary genres, memoir, adaptation and documentary. Description-only Renaissance Italy and Writing Art’s Histories add comparative visual culture and methods of interpretation. The third option responds to public culture and regional institutions through museum practice, collections and restitution, cultural heritage, comparative politics, policy analysis and social theory. Public Policy Analysis provides a real description-supported contribution in comparative policy processes and policy writing. It does not teach Frisian language policy. American media and history courses supply contextual methods, not regional Frisian evidence. These three substantive strands differ in central questions, core selections and methods. The workbook has no Frisian instruction or sustained Frisian studies, and beginner Dutch, bilingualism and literary work cannot implement the separate Frisian-specific direction. Rescheduling Psycholinguistics after Brain and Behavior and moving Rhetoric in Action to an offered term repair the closest option. The two more specific options retain literary or public-institution focus through academically stronger substitutions. Kept only three supported partial alignments, with the local thesis, internship and language specialism displayed separately.
